1	# Releasing Hey Reachy
2	
3	Signed artifacts are produced locally; CI only publishes the GitHub release with
4	generated notes. Credentials never enter the repository or CI.
5	
6	## One-time setup
7	
8	1. **App Store Connect API key** — App Store Connect → Users and Access →
9	   Integrations → App Store Connect API → Team Keys, role **App Manager**.
10	   Download the `.p8` once and write the credentials file:
11	
12	   ```bash
13	   mkdir -p ~/.config/reachy-mini
14	   cat > ~/.config/reachy-mini/release.env <<'CONF'
15	   REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=XXXXXXXXXX
16	   REACHY_ASC_KEY_ID=XXXXXXXXXX
17	   REACHY_ASC_ISSUER_ID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
18	   REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH=/Users/you/.config/reachy-mini/AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8
19	   CONF
20	   ```
21	
22	2. **App IDs and the App Group** — the first signed build with
23	   `-allowProvisioningUpdates` registers the bundle ids
24	   (`com.alexey1312.ReachyMini`, `.Widget`), but the
25	   `group.com.alexey1312.ReachyMini` capability must be added by hand in
26	   Xcode's Signing & Capabilities, once per App ID (app and widget separately,
27	   iOS and macOS separately). `xcodebuild` cannot create it.
28	
29	3. **App Store Connect app record** — My Apps → New App:
30	   - Name: **Hey Reachy**; if taken, fall back to “Hey Reachy — robot remote”.
31	   - Subtitle: **Control your Reachy Mini**.
32	   - Bundle id `com.alexey1312.ReachyMini`.
33	   - The description must state it is an unofficial client for Reachy Mini by
34	     Pollen Robotics. A public TestFlight link goes through Beta App Review, so
35	     the name is checked before any App Store submission.
36	   - App Privacy: no data collected. The app talks to the robot on the local
37	     network and to Hugging Face with the user's own OAuth session; nothing is
38	     sent to the developer.
39	   - Encryption: answered in the Info.plist (`ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption`),
40	     ASC asks nothing per build.
41	
42	4. **Developer ID Application certificate** (macOS) — Xcode → Settings →
43	   Accounts → Manage Certificates → “+” → Developer ID Application.
44	
45	5. **macOS ships through both channels**, so the Mac App Store one needs its own
46	   signing assets besides the Developer ID certificate: Apple Distribution and
47	   Mac Installer Distribution. `-allowProvisioningUpdates` creates them through
48	   the Xcode account the same way it does for iOS. The app record already
49	   carries a macOS platform beside the iOS one — `mise run asc -- versions list
50	   --app 6799644194` shows both — so nothing has to be created in App Store
51	   Connect. What is not automatic is the App Group: step 2 registers it per App
52	   ID, and the macOS App ID is a separate one from the iOS App ID.
53	
54	## Each release
55	
56	1. Bump `MARKETING_VERSION` in `Apps/Project.swift` (bare semver, e.g. `0.2.0`)
57	   and land it on `main`. Build numbers are the commit count — nothing to bump.
58	2. Tag and push; the tag triggers the GitHub release with git-cliff notes:
59	
60	   ```bash
61	   git tag 0.2.0 && git push origin 0.2.0
62	   ```
63	
64	3. Produce and ship the artifacts:
65	
66	   ```bash
67	   mise run release:ios     # archive → TestFlight
68	   mise run release:macos   # archive → both macOS channels (see below)
69	   gh release upload 0.2.0 Apps/DerivedData/Export/macOS/HeyReachy-0.2.0.zip
70	   ```
71	
72	`release:macos` archives once and exports that archive twice, because
73	`-exportArchive` re-signs per method — the two artifacts are the same build:
74	
75	| Channel        | Method            | Artifact                           | Ends up in              |
76	| -------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
77	| `developer-id` | notarize → staple | `Export/macOS/HeyReachy-<ver>.zip` | GitHub release, by hand |
78	| `appstore`     | upload            | `.pkg` (not kept)                  | TestFlight for macOS    |
79	
80	Developer ID runs first on purpose: it is the artifact that always ships, and a
81	failed App Store upload should not also cost you the zip. Pick one channel with
82	`--channel appstore` or `--channel developer-id`.
83	
84	Both archive commands compile with the Xcode compilation cache off
85	(`COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING=NO`) and then run
86	`Scripts/check-appintents-metadata.sh` against the archive before anything is
87	exported or uploaded. The intents live in a static SPM library, so the
88	Shortcuts app only ever sees what `appintentsmetadataprocessor` extracted into
89	`Metadata.appintents` — and extraction failing is a warning, never a build
90	error. TestFlight 0.1.1 shipped exactly that way: green archive, no actions in
91	the Shortcuts app. The check names every missing action instead; if it fails,
92	the fix is in the build, not in App Store Connect.
93	
94	Dry runs: `mise run release:ios -- --no-upload` exports an `.ipa` without
95	uploading; `mise run release:macos -- --no-notarize` stops the Developer ID
96	channel after the signed export, and `--no-upload` makes the App Store channel
97	leave a `.pkg` in `Export/macOS/AppStore` instead of uploading it. Each flag
98	belongs to one channel and is ignored by the other.
99	
100	## The public beta
101	
102	`https://testflight.apple.com/join/CGjefT9a` — the **Public Beta** group,
103	`c48f6abb-c178-40a2-8747-b6513add766e`, capped at 500 testers. The link is in
104	the README; raising the cap is one `groups edit --public-link-limit`, lowering
105	it below the people who already joined is not.
106	
107	Uploading is not distributing. An upload reaches the internal group by itself,
108	because `Internal` carries `hasAccessToAllBuilds`; the public group has to be
109	attached per build, per platform, and each one is its own Beta App Review:
110	
111	```bash
112	mise run asc -- builds add-groups --app 6799644194 --latest --platform IOS \
113	  --group c48f6abb-c178-40a2-8747-b6513add766e --submit --confirm
114	mise run asc -- builds add-groups --app 6799644194 --latest --platform MAC_OS \
115	  --group c48f6abb-c178-40a2-8747-b6513add766e --submit --confirm
116	mise run asc -- testflight review submissions list --build-id "<id>"
117	```
118	
119	What review reads lives at the app level, not the build level, so it is written
120	once and stays: the tester-facing text in `testflight app-localizations`
121	(description, feedback email, marketing URL, and the privacy policy at
122	`docs/privacy.md` — which has to resolve on `main`, or review fails on a 404),
123	and the reviewer-facing contact and notes in `testflight review edit`. The notes
124	carry the thing no reviewer can guess — that the app needs a robot nobody at
125	Apple has, that the Bluetooth sheet auto-presenting on first launch hides the
126	Local Network alert underneath it, and that Hugging Face sign-in is the one path
127	that completes without hardware. Beta App Review has no demo account to give,
128	because the app has no accounts.
129	
130	Testers see the same What to Test note per build:
131	
132	```bash
133	mise run asc -- builds test-notes create --build-id "<id>" \
134	  --locale en-US --whats-new "..."
135	```
136	
137	## Querying App Store Connect
138	
139	`mise run asc` is the App Store Connect CLI with the same key already loaded —
140	`Scripts/asc.sh` maps the `REACHY_ASC_*` values onto the `ASC_*` names the tool
141	reads, so nothing is stored twice and no keychain profile exists to drift.
142	Everything after `--` goes to `asc`:
143	
144	```bash
145	mise run asc -- apps list
146	mise run asc -- builds list --app 6799644194   # did the TestFlight upload land?
147	mise run asc -- testflight beta-groups list --app 6799644194
148	```
149	
150	`asc` resolves a stored profile before the environment, so an `asc auth login`
151	run by hand silently outranks this wrapper — `mise run asc -- auth status`
152	prints which of the two is answering. The key is App Manager, not Admin, so the
153	same limit release-ios.sh documents applies: it can read and submit, and it
154	cannot manage provisioning profiles.
155	
156	The CLI also ships 23 agent skills (`asc install-skills`, pinned to a reviewed
157	commit) covering TestFlight, metadata, submissions and signing.
158	
159	## Xcode Cloud (optional, continuous TestFlight)
160	
161	`Apps/ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh` makes a generated project buildable on
162	Xcode Cloud: it installs the pinned tools through the committed `bin/mise`
163	bootstrap, generates the workspace, and stamps `CI_BUILD_NUMBER` in as the
164	build number. Signing there is managed by Apple — no certificates leave the
165	account — and TestFlight distribution is a post-action checkbox. The setup
166	quirks (create the workflow from a local Xcode, start the build counter above
167	the last local upload, Git LFS is unsupported so never build the snapshot
168	scheme there) are commented at the top of the script.
169

#!/bin/bash
# Archive the iOS app (Release, signed) and upload it to TestFlight.
#
#   mise run release:ios              # archive → upload to App Store Connect
#   mise run release:ios -- --no-upload   # archive → export an .ipa locally
#
# Signing and uploading go through the Xcode account, not the App Store Connect
# API key — see release-env.sh for the measurement behind that.
#
# The build number is the commit count: monotonic, reproducible, and never
# stored in the repository — so releasing does not require a version-bump
# commit for anything but MARKETING_VERSION.
set -euo pipefail

# shellcheck source=Scripts/release-env.sh
. "$(dirname "$0")/release-env.sh"

upload=true
require_development_team
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
  --no-upload) upload=false ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: release-ios.sh [--no-upload]" >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
  esac
  shift
done

BUILD_NUMBER="$(git rev-list --count HEAD)"
ARCHIVE=Apps/DerivedData/Archives/ReachyMini-iOS.xcarchive

set -o pipefail
# COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING=NO: the shipping artifact gets a clean,
# uncached compile. The cache went on by default the day before 0.1.1 was
# archived, and 0.1.1 is the build that installed from TestFlight with no
# Shortcuts actions at all — an archive is rare enough that replayed
# compilations buy nothing worth that variable. The metadata check below is
# what proves the archive either way, before anything is uploaded.
xcodebuild archive \
  -workspace Apps/ReachyMiniApps.xcworkspace -scheme ReachyMini \
  -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' -configuration Release \
  -archivePath "$ARCHIVE" -derivedDataPath Apps/DerivedData \
  DEVELOPMENT_TEAM="$REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM" CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic \
  CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION="$BUILD_NUMBER" \
  COMPILATION_CACHE_ENABLE_CACHING=NO \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  -skipPackagePluginValidation -skipMacroValidation \
  2>&1 | xcsift

# An archive whose Metadata.appintents came out empty ships an app with no
# actions in the Shortcuts app, and nothing in the build reddens over it.
Scripts/check-appintents-metadata.sh "$ARCHIVE"

EXPORT_OPTIONS="$(appstore_export_options "$upload")"

xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath "$ARCHIVE" \
  -exportOptionsPlist "$EXPORT_OPTIONS" \
  -exportPath Apps/DerivedData/Export/iOS \
  -allowProvisioningUpdates \
  2>&1 | xcsift

if [ "$upload" = true ]; then
  echo "Uploaded build $BUILD_NUMBER to App Store Connect. TestFlight shows it after processing (minutes)."
else
  # The archive was already checked, but the .ipa is what actually ships, and
  # -exportArchive re-signs and repacks on the way — so prove the metadata
  # survived the export too. Only the --no-upload path leaves an .ipa behind;
  # `destination: upload` hands the artifact straight to App Store Connect.
  IPA="$(ls Apps/DerivedData/Export/iOS/*.ipa | head -1)"
  UNPACKED="$(mktemp -d -t reachy-ipa-check)"
  ditto -x -k "$IPA" "$UNPACKED"
  Scripts/check-appintents-metadata.sh "$UNPACKED"/Payload/*.app
  echo "Exported without uploading:"
  ls Apps/DerivedData/Export/iOS/*.ipa
fi

#!/bin/bash
# Sourced by release-ios.sh, release-macos.sh and asc.sh: loads and checks the
# release credentials. Like the device signing team, they live outside every worktree in
# ~/.config/reachy-mini/, so nothing is copied when a workspace is created and
# nothing account-specific ever lands in the repository.
#
# Exported variables win over the file, so a CI machine can inject its own.

RELEASE_CONFIG="${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/reachy-mini/release.env"
DEVICE_CONFIG="${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/reachy-mini/device.env"

# The signing team is the same one device builds already use; read it first so
# release.env only has to add the App Store Connect key.
if [ -z "${REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM:-}" ] && [ -f "$DEVICE_CONFIG" ]; then
  # shellcheck disable=SC1090
  . "$DEVICE_CONFIG"
fi
if [ -f "$RELEASE_CONFIG" ]; then
  # shellcheck disable=SC1090
  . "$RELEASE_CONFIG"
fi

# Demanded by the two scripts that archive; asc.sh sources this file for the API key
# alone and never signs anything, so the check cannot run on load.
require_development_team() {
  [ -n "${REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM:-}" ] && return 0
  cat >&2 <<EOF
No signing team. Write it once, the way device builds already expect:

  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$DEVICE_CONFIG")"
  echo 'REACHY_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=XXXXXXXXXX' > "$DEVICE_CONFIG"

The id is in Xcode → Settings → Accounts, next to the team that owns com.alexey1312.*.
EOF
  exit 1
}

# The API key is optional, and deliberately unused for signing. xcodebuild takes
# `-authenticationKey*` as "do everything through cloud signing", and a key below
# the Admin role cannot manage profiles — the export then fails with "Cloud
# signing permission error" and "No profiles were found" even though the
# certificate is right there in the keychain. A key's role cannot be changed
# after it is created. Without the flags xcodebuild uses the Xcode account, which
# has the rights, so signing is left to it and the key is kept for the two things
# that only need to read and submit: notarization, and CI.
REACHY_HAS_ASC=""
if [ -n "${REACHY_ASC_KEY_ID:-}" ] && [ -n "${REACHY_ASC_ISSUER_ID:-}" ] && [ -n "${REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH:-}" ]; then
  if [ ! -f "$REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH" ]; then
    echo "REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH points at $REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH, which does not exist." >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  REACHY_HAS_ASC=1
fi

# `destination: upload` in the shared plist is what hands the artifact to App Store
# Connect, and it is the only key a dry run has to change. Generating the copy beats
# keeping a second file, which would drift the moment either channel gains an option.
# Takes the value of the caller's own upload flag and echoes the plist to use.
appstore_export_options() {
  if [ "${1:-true}" = true ]; then
    echo Scripts/exportOptions/appstore.plist
    return 0
  fi
  local options
  options="$(mktemp -t reachy-export-options).plist"
  plutil -convert xml1 -o "$options" Scripts/exportOptions/appstore.plist
  plutil -replace destination -string export "$options"
  echo "$options"
}

# Called by the macOS script, where notarytool has no other way in, and by asc.sh,
# which is nothing but the key.
require_asc_key() {
  [ -n "$REACHY_HAS_ASC" ] && return 0
  cat >&2 <<EOF
This needs an App Store Connect API key (App Store Connect → Users and Access →
Integrations → App Store Connect API). Write the three values once:

  cat >> "$RELEASE_CONFIG" <<'CONF'
REACHY_ASC_KEY_ID=XXXXXXXXXX
REACHY_ASC_ISSUER_ID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
REACHY_ASC_KEY_PATH=$HOME/.config/reachy-mini/AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8
CONF

The one-time App Store Connect setup is documented in docs/release.md.
EOF
  exit 1
}

feat(intents): play a move from Siri, name the robot, reach the Lock Screen (#82)
* feat(cache): put the catalogue cache in the App Group container

`RobotCatalogueCache.default` was rooted at the process's own caches
directory, so an App Intent running in the widget's process read a
different directory and found nothing. The apps slot never showed it —
the widget reads `RobotAppsCacheStore`, which has been in the group suite
all along — but the moves slot has no such twin, and a move picker with
nothing in it is what surfaced it.

`KnownRobots.appGroupIdentifier` is now the one answer to "which group",
read by the shared suite and the shared container alike, so a bundle
naming none degrades both the same way.

Nothing is migrated: every record here is recoverable from the robot, so
the cost is one Hugging Face round trip on the first connection after the
update.

* feat(intents): give every intent a robot to address

`RobotIntentTarget` meant "the last known robot", which works with one
robot on the desk and stops working the moment there are two. Every
discoverable intent now takes an optional `RobotEntity`, and
`RobotEntityQuery` fills the picker out of `KnownRobots` — no network,
because a robot is not less known for being switched off.

The entity contributes an identity and never an address: a shortcut is
persisted once and the same robot answers somewhere else tomorrow, so
`knownRobot(id:)` looks it up when the intent runs. A robot the app has
since forgotten refuses rather than retargeting silently.

Optional on all six existing intents, which is what kept their phrases
working — read back off the built `extract.actionsdata`: eight actions,
six `autoShortcuts`, `RobotEntity` optional on each.

* feat(moves): play a recorded move from Siri and Shortcuts

Moves had no intent coverage at all — the tab was reachable only by
opening the app — while the daemon route behind it is a single call and
the move index already survives across launches.

`MoveEntity` is addressed as `dataset#move`, which makes it the one
entity here that resolves with no cache and no robot: a year-old shortcut
still runs against a sleeping Reachy. `MoveEntityQuery` fills the picker
out of `RobotCatalogueCache` and never writes it — `persistMoveIndex`
carries the index's date across each write so it ages as one unit, and a
second writer would re-date every library the app had merely read.

`RobotMovePlayer` is the robot half, and both of its steps exist because
the daemon fails silently without them: a play route never touches the
motor mode, so an asleep robot makes the sound and does not move, and
`play_move` takes its guard non-blocking, so a play over a running move
is accepted and moves nothing. Both are pinned by mutation.

Eight of the ten App Shortcut slots are now spent; the new intents are in
`check-appintents-metadata.sh`, and the built metadata reads back ten
actions, eight autoShortcuts and `MoveEntity` registered.

* feat(widget): put the robot on the Lock Screen and StandBy

The status widget shipped two families. It now offers the three accessory
ones as well, which is also the groundwork for a watch complication.

`RobotWidgetView` already took its layout as a parameter, so this is new
cases and new views. What was not free is `RobotStatusProvider.layout`:
it read `family == .systemSmall ? .compact : .wide`, so declaring a
family nobody had thought about would have rendered a 338 pt row inside a
76 pt ring, silently. It is exhaustive now.

Each family shows a different half of the reading, and the recordings are
what decided which. Rectangular has room for the robot's name over its
state. Circular carried the name at first and came back with "kitchen"
clipped to "kitcher", then with the glyph's head cut off by the ring — it
is a glyph alone now, sized to the ring rather than to a type step, with
the words spoken to VoiceOver. Inline shows the state rather than the
name, because that line sits beside the clock and the name is the one
thing its owner already knows.

None of the three carries the wake/sleep button. `.accessoryInline`
could not — the system builds that line itself and discards a `Button` —
and the other two are a decision: a ring holding a capsule has nothing
left to say what the robot is doing. The whole surface falls through to
`widgetURL`.

The references that follow prove the layout and the wording, not the
rendering: `AccessoryWidgetBackground` is a system material and a
material does not render headless. The Lock Screen's vibrant treatment is
a device check.

* test(snapshots): record the accessory widget references

Forty-four images: eleven previews across three families, two devices and
both appearances. Nothing else moved — not one of the ~1100 existing
references was rewritten, which is worth saying because a wide sweep after
adding previews is the normal outcome here and this was not one.

They were written by `test:snapshots` itself rather than by `record`:
Prefire generates `record: .missing`, so a reference that does not exist
is created instead of compared, and `record` — which deletes every PNG
first — was never needed.

* fix(intents): believe a snapshot only about the robot the intent named

Everything the app does over Bluetooth was written against `bluetooth_service.py` in daemon 1.9.0 (read from

carries about 182. The robot's `WriteValue` ignores `options["offset"]`, so a value CoreBluetooth splits into ATT
prepare/execute writes arrives as _two separate commands_, not as one reassembled payload. If it does not fit, the
Bluetooth path cannot provision at all and the HTTP path through `reachy-mini-ap` becomes the only one.

- [ ] `maximumWriteValueLength(for: .withoutResponse)` — the single-packet budget the pump enforces.

- `metadata/version/<version>/<locale>.json` for version fields: `description`, `keywords`, `marketingUrl`, `promotionalText`, `supportUrl`, `whatsNew`


Most of the app sits behind a live connection to a robot, and we have no way to hand you one. With no Reachy Mini on the same Wi-Fi network the app stays on its Connect screen: the five main tabs (Robot, Live, Moves, Apps, Settings) are not instantiated until a handshake with a robot's daemon succeeds. There is no demo mode, no mock data and no test account, because the app has no backend of its own and no accounts of its own. The App Store description states this requirement in its second paragraph.

FIRST LAUNCH, PLEASE READ

A Bluetooth setup sheet opens automatically over the Connect screen on the very first launch. Dismiss it with Cancel: the iOS Local Network permission alert is waiting underneath it. Please allow that one. The app uses Bonjour to find robots on the local network and does nothing else with it.

WHAT YOU CAN EVALUATE WITHOUT THE ROBOT

1. Connect screen. Three segments: "This network" (Bonjour discovery, which will stay on "Searching..."), "Hugging Face", and "Manual". Under Manual, type any host and tap Connect to exercise the real failure path ("Couldn't connect to ...", Try again, Cancel).

Microphone: only to talk through the robot's speaker during a live session, requested on demand.
